question: Which of the following is NOT an example of 'fiat' money in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __Rs. 1000 cheque.__

__
 
• Fiat money __

 __
 
• Government-issued currency known as "fiat money" is not backed by a physical good like gold. Because they can manage the amount of money printed, central banks using fiat money have more power over the economy. The majority of contemporary paper currencies, including the dollar, are fiat currencies.
 
• Fiat money, which was introduced as a replacement for representational money and commodity money, has a value based on supply and demand.
 
• Commodity money is created from precious metals such as gold and silver, while representative money represents a claim on a commodity that can be redeemed.
 
• Around the year 1000 AD, China became the first nation to employ fiat money, after which other nations began to use it as well. As a result of President Richard Nixon's law repealing the direct convertibility of the US dollar into gold, it gained popularity in the 20th century. The majority of countries currently employ paper-based fiat currencies that only serve as a mode of payment. 
 
 
 
• History of Fiat Money__
 __
 
• In the 10th century, mostly under the Yuan, Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties, China is where fiat money first appeared. Metal money was in great demand during the Tang Dynasty (618–907) and was harder to come by than precious metals. The populace was accustomed to using credit notes, and paper or paper draughts were commonly accepted.
 
• People were obliged to switch from coins to notes due to a coin shortage. The Sichuan province experienced a boom in trade during the Song Dynasty (960–1276), which resulted in a dearth of copper coins. Private notes backed by a monetary reserve were originally recognised as legal money when traders began issuing them. The only legal tender in the became paper money Yuan Dynasty (1276-1367), and issuing of notes was conferred to the Ministry of Finance during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644).
 
• According to the Bretton Woods Agreement, a troy ounce of gold is worth 35 US dollars. However, due to diminishing gold reserves, US President Richard Nixon implemented a number of economic measures in 1971, including ending the direct conversion of US dollars into gold. Since then, the majority of nations have adopted fiat currencies that can be exchanged for other significant currencies.

• Advantages and disadvantages of Fiat Money-
 
 
• 
 
In the 20th century, governments and banks intervened to shield their economies from the recurrent business cycle busts, which led to the widespread usage of fiat money.

 
Disadvantage- Currency based on commodities was unstable because of the regular business cycle and cyclical recessions. The central banks have more control over the money supply, interest rates, and liquidity since they can produce or hold paper money as needed. For instance, the Federal Reserve was able to handle the World Banking Crisis of 2008 to prevent more damage to the U.S. financial system and the global economy because to its control over the money supply and demand.

 
Advantage- The global financial crisis disproved the notion that fiat money is a more stable currency that can protect against recessions. Regardless of the Federal Reserve controls the money supply, it was not able to prevent the crisis from happening. Critics of fiat money argue that the limited supply of gold makes it a more stable currency than fiat money, which has an unlimited supply.
